title.en: Powers, exponents and the Power Play

text.en: Estu says paper cannot be folded more than 7 times. Roxie asks what happens with thinner paper, and says that 46 folds of a sheet would reach the Moon!

If a sheet is 0.001 cm thick, each fold doubles the thickness, so after 1 fold it is 0.002 cm, after 2 folds 0.004 cm and after 3 folds 0.008 cm.
After 10 folds the thickness is only 1.024 cm, after 17 folds about 131 cm, after 30 folds about 10.7 km, and after 46 folds more than 7,00,000 km.
This repeated doubling is called multiplicative or exponential growth, and it explodes far faster than adding the same amount each time.
We write repeated multiplication with a power: 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 2⁴, where 2 is the base and 4 is the exponent.
The thickness after n folds is 0.001 cm × 2ⁿ, which is a short formula for a long multiplication.
To multiply powers with the same base, add the exponents: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n).
To divide powers with the same base, subtract the exponents: a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n).
A power of a power multiplies the exponents: (a^m)^n = a^(mn).
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, and a negative exponent means the reciprocal: a^(−n) = 1/aⁿ.
Powers of 10 help us write very large and very small numbers, so 3,00,000 = 3 × 10⁵ and 0.0004 = 4 × 10⁻⁴.

Same base, so the exponents subtract: 8 − 4 = 4.

prompt.en: Why does paper folded 46 times become so thick?

requiredIdeas.en: Doubling 46 times gives 2⁴⁶, a huge multiplier.

commonMisconceptions.en: Doubling 46 times is only 92 times the thickness.

points.en: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ.
Powers of 10 write huge and tiny numbers compactly.
